title: C# for a senior engineer who already ships .NET
hook: C# is a compiled, statically typed language that runs on the CLR. You already use it in .NET microservices; this track rebuilds the language from compilation up to GC and concurrency so interview answers stay precise.

sections.heading: What C# actually is
sections.prose: Microsoft’s tour of C# describes it as a modern, object-oriented, type-safe language that also supports functional techniques, LINQ, and async. You write C# source; the compiler emits IL into assemblies; the common language runtime (CLR) loads that IL and either JIT-compiles it or uses Native AOT. That is a different world from TypeScript, which erases types and emits JavaScript for a JS engine. C# types survive as metadata. The CLR uses them for safety at run time. The Common Type System (CTS) is the shared type model for .NET languages. The Base Class Library (BCL) is the set of types you import — List, Task, String, HttpClient — not the language itself. Interviews mix these layers. This track keeps them named so you can say “that is the language” versus “that is the runtime” versus “that is ASP.NET,” which belongs in the later .NET framework docs.

snippets.label: A complete C# 14 file-scoped program
snippets.explanation: Top-level statements compile to a synthesized entry point. The language still has types, a compilation step, and a CLR host — unlike a Node .mjs file that the engine parses directly.

sections.heading: How this differs from JavaScript and TypeScript
sections.prose: JavaScript is dynamically typed and JIT-compiled by V8 or similar. TypeScript adds a compile-time checker and then disappears. C# keeps types in the assembly. Value types versus reference types are a language-and-CLR contract, not a documentation comment. Privacy modifiers are enforced by the runtime, not erased. async/await in C# builds a state machine over Task, not over Promises. Garbage collection exists in both V8 and the CLR, but the knobs (generations, LOH, server GC) are different. When a page correlates a concept, it uses a futureTopicSlug such as javascript/async/event-loop so the later JS/TS tracks can link back.

sections.heading: How to study this index
sections.prose: Modules are numbered in learning order, not interview-topic popularity. Foundations (01–07) make you fluent in reading and writing correct C#. Intermediate (08–13) is daily production: collections, generics, delegates, patterns, LINQ, async. Advanced (14–18) is the depth interviewers use to separate “I used C# for five years” from “I can explain the CLR.” Each module ends with a mind map, a one-screen quick overview, and an interview page. Modern features (records, init, collection expressions, C# 14 field-backed properties) are taught in the module they belong to, with introducedIn set. Module 18 is a recap map, not the first lesson. Primary target is C# 14 on .NET 10.

sections.heading: Examples from your work
sections.prose: Snippets are not toy inventories. They use shapes you have shipped: SQS and EventBridge consumers, Redis cache keys, RabbitMQ offload, SkiaSharp dispose, LTI/auth provider branching, bulk CSV import, and the 199-to-999 concurrent attempt-submit path. ASP.NET Core controllers and EF Core stay out of this track.

stages.title: Foundations (01–07)
stages.summary: Program, syntax, types, members, OOP, exceptions, null safety. Finish this before LINQ or threading.

stages.title: Intermediate (08–13)
stages.summary: Collections, generics, delegates, pattern matching, LINQ, async/await — the code you write in workers every week.

stages.title: Advanced (14–18)
stages.summary: GC, threading, reflection, Span/unsafe, then a C# 8–14 recap and performance idioms.

timeMaps.focus: Still start at foundations. Skim 01–03, then 05 (OOP uniqueness), 06 (using/IDisposable), and 07 (NRT). Do not jump to GC first.
Complete 01–13 with interview pages. That covers daily C# plus async. Leave 14–18 for a third sitting.
All 18 modules in order. Use mind maps and interview pages as revision, not as a substitute for the topic pages.
